questions.prompt: The glomerular filtration rate (GFR) can be measured using the renal clearance of a substance that is freely filtered across the glomerular capillaries but is neither reabsorbed nor secreted by the renal tubules.
A selective constriction of the efferent arteriole will lead to a decrease in the filtration fraction because renal plasma flow (RPF) decreases more significantly than GFR.
In a patient with an obstructing ureteral stone, the primary cause of the decrease in GFR is a significant increase in the hydrostatic pressure within Bowman's space.
Autoregulation of renal blood flow (RBF) remains effective even in a denervated, transplanted kidney because the mechanisms are intrinsic to the renal vasculature.
The clearance of para-aminohippuric acid (PAH) provides an accurate estimate of the true renal blood flow because it is completely removed from the plasma in a single pass.
At plasma glucose concentrations exceeding the transport maximum (Tm), the rate of glucose reabsorption continues to rise linearly with any further increase in plasma concentration.
A clearance ratio of substance x to inulin (C_x/C_inulin) equal to 0.7 indicates that there has been net secretion of substance x into the renal tubules.
If a freely filtered substance x has a [TF/P]_x /[TF/P]_inulin  ratio of 1.1 at the end of the proximal tubule, it can be concluded that the substance has undergone net reabsorption in that segment.
Approximately 67% of the filtered sodium is reabsorbed in the proximal convoluted tubule via a process that is strictly isosmotic, meaning water is reabsorbed in exact proportion to solute.
Extracellular fluid (ECF) volume expansion increases the hydrostatic pressure and decreases the oncotic pressure of peritubular capillary blood, which inhibits proximal tubular reabsorption.
In a patient with Addison's disease, the characteristic hyponatremia is primarily caused by an osmotic shift of sodium ions from the extracellular fluid into the intracellular fluid.
Glomerulotubular balance is a mechanism ensuring that if the GFR decreases, the absolute rate of proximal reabsorption increases to prevent excessive loss of sodium.
The thick ascending limb of the loop of Henle remains impermeable to water regardless of the circulating levels of antidiuretic hormone (ADH).
The "single effect" of countercurrent multiplication in the loop of Henle causes the osmolarity of the tubular fluid in the thick ascending limb to increase relative to the interstitium.
Loop diuretics such as furosemide increase the urinary excretion of calcium by abolishing the lumen-positive potential difference that normally drives paracellular calcium reabsorption.
In the presence of high levels of ADH, the urea concentration in the inner medullary interstitium decreases because urea is trapped within the collecting ducts.
Most of the body's total potassium content is located in the extracellular fluid to facilitate the rapid generation of action potentials in nerve and muscle.
Insulin assists in maintaining internal potassium balance by stimulating the Na^+/K^+ ATPase pump to move potassium from the ECF into the cells.
Acute metabolic alkalosis is a common cause of hyperkalemia because hydrogen ions exit the cells in exchange for potassium entering the cells.
A high-potassium diet increases the rate of potassium secretion by principal cells by raising the intracellular potassium concentration and increasing the chemical driving force for secretion.
ADH regulates water reabsorption by directing the insertion of aquaporin-2 channels into the luminal membranes of the principal cells in the late distal tubule and collecting duct.
Central diabetes insipidus is a condition where the posterior pituitary gland secretes excessive amounts of ADH that cannot be sensed by the renal collecting ducts.
In the syndrome of inappropriate ADH (SIADH), the extracellular fluid volume is significantly decreased due to the movement of water into the intracellular compartment.
During a period of severe water deprivation, the [TF/P]_osmolarity ratio measured at the end of the proximal convoluted tubule will be significantly greater than 1.0.
The primary site for the reabsorption of filtered bicarbonate ions is the distal convoluted tubule, where H^+-ATPase pumps are most active.
For every hydrogen ion excreted as titratable acid, one molecule of "new" bicarbonate is synthesized in the renal cell and reabsorbed into the peritubular capillary blood.
In patients with chronic renal failure, the metabolic acidosis is primarily caused by a failure to excrete the daily load of fixed hydrogen ions as ammonium (NH4+).
Hyperkalemia stimulates the synthesis of ammonia (NH3) from glutamine in the proximal tubule to help compensate for metabolic acidosis.
Mannitol is the preferred clinical marker for measuring the volume of the total body water because it distributes uniformly across all fluid compartments.
In hyposmotic volume expansion, such as that seen in SIADH, both the intracellular and extracellular fluid volumes are increased while their osmolarities are decreased.
An intravenous infusion of a 3% NaCl solution will cause water to shift from the intracellular compartment to the extracellular compartment until osmotic equilibrium is reached.
In isosmotic volume contraction, such as during an episode of diarrhea, the hematocrit increases because the loss of extracellular fluid concentrates the red blood cells.
Parathyroid hormone  increases the renal reabsorption of phosphate in the proximal tubule by up-regulating Na + -phosphate cotransporters.
The myogenic hypothesis of renal autoregulation suggests that afferent arteriolar smooth muscle relaxes in response to an increase in wall stretch.
Thiazide diuretics are effective in treating idiopathic hypercalciuria because they inhibit Na^+-Cl^- cotransport and simultaneously increase calcium reabsorption in the early distal tubule.
A patient presenting with a fractional excretion of sodium (FE Na ) of less than 1% and a BUN/creatinine ratio greater than 20:1 is likely suffering from prerenal azotemia.
The corticopapillary osmotic gradient, which is essential for urine concentration, is composed primarily of accumulated sodium chloride and urea.
Urea recycling from the inner medullary collecting ducts into the interstitium is facilitated by ADH and contributes to the medullary osmotic gradient.
A patient with nephrogenic diabetes insipidus will typically show a large increase in urine osmolarity within one hour of receiving an injection of dDAVP.
If the plasma protein concentration increases significantly, the glomerular capillary oncotic pressure will rise, leading to a decrease in the net ultrafiltration pressure and GFR.
Renal prostaglandins E2  and I2  act as vasodilators to prevent profound reductions in RBF in states of high sympathetic nerve activity, such as hemorrhage.
The filtration fraction is defined physiologically as the ratio of the total renal blood flow to the glomerular filtration rate.
The vasa recta function as countercurrent exchangers, a passive process that prevents the dissipation of the corticopapillary osmotic gradient by the blood flow.
Angiotensin II contributes to Na^+ balance by stimulating Na + -H +  exchange in the proximal convoluted tubule, which increases the reabsorption of sodium and bicarbonate.
The minimum urinary pH that the renal transport mechanisms can maintain against a concentration gradient is approximately 6.0.
In the glucose titration curve, "splay" refers to the appearance of glucose in the urine before the average transport maximum for the kidney is reached.
In a state of hyperosmotic volume contraction, such as profuse sweating, the hematocrit typically increases significantly because red blood cells swell.
Atrial natriuretic peptide (ANP) increases the GFR by simultaneously dilating the afferent arterioles and constricting the efferent arterioles.
Under normal resting conditions, the vasa recta receive approximately 25% of the total renal blood flow to ensure efficient countercurrent exchange.
The process of "diffusion trapping" involves the conversion of lipid-soluble NH3 to water-soluble NH4+ in the tubular lumen, which ensures its excretion in the urine.
